name: Reciprocity
statement: People who have received an unsolicited gift, favour or concession comply more often with a later request from whoever gave it.
meaning: Three separate literatures answer to the word reciprocity, and they do not share a method or a claim. The first is sociological. Alvin Gouldner argued in 1960 that a moral norm requiring the return of benefits is one of the universal components of moral codes, and he separated three things usually run together: reciprocity as a pattern of mutually contingent exchange, the folk belief that people get what they deserve, and the generalised moral norm itself. The second is the compliance literature. Dennis Regan showed in 1971 that an unrequested favour raises compliance with a later request, and that liking for the favour-doer does not explain the rise. The third is economic. Reciprocity is modelled as a preference, tested in bargaining and investment games, and taken to explain why people repay kindness at a cost to themselves. Claims proved in one of these three do not transfer to the others, and the compliance techniques marketed under the name have the weakest evidence of the three.

origin.note: The paper is "The norm of reciprocity: A preliminary statement", 25(2), 161-178. It contains no experiment. Gouldner wrote it as an attack on functionalism, specifically on that school's failure to handle power and unequal exchange, and he said so in a 1979 note on the paper for Current Contents. The first experiment on reciprocity as a compliance lever is Regan's, eleven years later, and the door-in-the-face technique was named by Robert Cialdini and five colleagues in 1975.

evidence: Regan recruited 81 male Stanford freshmen for a study advertised as being about aesthetics, and analysed 77. A confederate either brought the subject an unrequested Coca-Cola, or the experimenter handed out Cokes to both, or nobody received anything. The confederate later passed a note asking the subject to buy raffle tickets at 25 cents each toward a new gym, the prize a Corvette. Mean purchases were 1.73 tickets after the confederate's favour, 1.08 after the experimenter's, and 0.92 after none, t = 2.28 and t = 3.11 against the two controls. The two control conditions did not differ, which rules out mood or modelled generosity. Liking for the confederate correlated with compliance among control subjects at r = .46, and among subjects who had received the favour at r = .14, not significant. Cialdini and colleagues introduced the door-in-the-face procedure in 1975: refuse a large request first, and compliance with the smaller one that follows rises. In their Study 3, 54.1% agreed to the smaller request after rejecting the extreme one, against 33.3% in each of two controls. Field work followed the same logic. Strohmetz, Rind, Fisher and Lynn had two waiters in Ithaca give each diner a foil-wrapped chocolate with the bill, and 92 dining parties tipped 17.8% with the chocolate against 15.1% without, t(90) = 5.25. Armin Falk ran the largest test. A children's charity in Zurich sent 9,846 Christmas solicitation letters for a school project in Dhaka, randomly assigning each to no gift, one postcard, or four postcards. Donation rates were 12%, 14% and 21%, giving 397, 465 and 691 donors from 3,262, 3,237 and 3,347 letters. The economic literature reaches the norm from the other direction, by watching people pay to punish or repay strangers. Oosterbeek, Sloof and Van De Kuilen pooled 75 results from 37 ultimatum-game papers and found that proposers offer 40% of the pie on average and responders reject 16% of offers.

replication.headline: A preregistered replication of the 1975 door-in-the-face study 45 years later found 51.3% compliance against 33.6% in the controls, and the meta-analytic effect across 89 comparisons is r = .14.
replication.detail: Genschow and six colleagues repeated Cialdini et al.'s Study 3 on a German campus with 391 analysed participants, having powered the study at .90. Compliance with the smaller request was 51.28% after rejecting the extreme request and 33.58% across the two combined controls, chi-squared = 10.82, p = .001. Against the equivalent-request control alone the figures were 51.28% and 29.58%, chi-squared = 12.66, p < .001, which the authors read as support for reciprocal concessions over the rival account that people simply avoid refusing twice. The original and replication percentages sit close together: 54.1 against 51.3 in the treatment, 33.3 against 29.6 and 37.9 in the controls. The meta-analytic record is weaker than any single study. O'Keefe and Hale pooled 88 request pairs and 7,780 participants in 1998 and found a random-effects mean of r = .097, 95% CI .049 to .144, and repeated the exercise in 2001 on 87 pairs using odds ratios, getting 1.46, 95% CI 1.18 to 1.82. Feeley, Anker and Aloe reported r = .126 across 78 comparisons for verbal compliance and r = .052 across 39 for behavioural compliance, the latter not significant. Feeley's 2025 update gives r = .14 across 89 verbal comparisons and r = .08 across 53 behavioural ones. Falk's postcard experiment is the field replication of the favour effect rather than the concession effect, and its treatment effects were significant at the 1% level in a probit on all 9,846 observations.

study.cite: Genschow, O., Westfal, M., Crusius, J., Bartosch, L., Feikes, K. I., Pallasch, N., & Wozniak, M. (2021). Does social psychology persist over half a century? A direct replication of Cialdini et al.'s (1975) classic door-in-the-face technique. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 120(2), e1-e7.

limits: The compliance technique is small and conditional even where it works. O'Keefe and Hale classified their 88 cases by five moderators, and where all five were favourable the mean was r = .152, while the other 43 cases averaged r = .039 and were not distinguishable from zero. The same split appears in the odds-ratio analysis: 1.86 under favourable conditions, 1.16 otherwise. Door-in-the-face effects are dependably positive only when the same person makes both requests, the beneficiary is the same, the cause is prosocial, the approach is face to face and there is no delay. Both O'Keefe and Hale reviews found effect size unrelated to the size of the concession, which is the one thing the reciprocal-concessions account predicts should matter. The behavioural evidence is thinner than the verbal evidence in both of Feeley's meta-analyses. Whether any of these reviews corrected for publication bias could not be checked: the 2012 and 2025 papers are paywalled and their abstracts do not mention it, and the 1998 review, which was read in full, runs no funnel or trim-and-fill test, though it did include unpublished dissertations that the two reviews before it had excluded. The restaurant work is small. Experiment 1 covered 92 dining parties at one Ithaca restaurant with two waiters, Experiment 2 covered 80 parties at one New Jersey restaurant with one server, and the servers knew which condition they were in. Regan's liking manipulation was weak by his own account, and he warns that the unpleasant condition was closer to a disliking manipulation than a liking one. Falk's gifts raised the number of donors and slightly lowered the size of the typical donation: the no-gift and large-gift distributions differ on a Kolmogorov-Smirnov test at p = .049. Gouldner's paper itself was read only through his own later summary of it and its Crossref record, not in full.
misreadings: The restaurant study is about chocolate, not mints. Experiment 1 used a fancy foil-wrapped piece chosen to be distinct from the wrapped mints restaurants hand out anyway, and Experiment 2 used Hershey miniatures from a basket. The four condition means in Experiment 2 were 18.95%, 19.59%, 21.62% and 22.99% on 20 parties each. The paper prints no percentage-increase figures for those four conditions, so the tidy sequence the study is usually quoted for comes from arithmetic done elsewhere. The one increase it does state is 21%, for what the server's total tips would have been had every party got the two-stage offer. Verbal compliance is not behaviour. Feeley, Anker and Aloe found the door-in-the-face raised stated agreement and left actual follow-through unmoved, which matters because the technique is sold on the strength of the second. Reciprocity as a norm and reciprocity as a trick are separate claims with separate evidence. Gouldner wrote a critique of functionalist theory and offered no persuasion advice, and his own summary lists three distinct things the word covers. Regan's result is often reported as showing that favours make people like you, and it shows the opposite of what that implies. Liking rose, and liking did not carry the effect: the correlation between liking and ticket purchases vanished in exactly the condition where the favour had been given.
